name: Lena Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start by checking the kit and the pole numbers before we take the bucket truck out. The best moment is seeing a row of homes light up again; the hard part is that I'm still a junior, and a wrong joint can cost a more experienced worker time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little AI can spare us from rewriting the same outage note three times, provided a lineworker checks every safety detail. I use a drafting tool daily for plain-language notes, but nobody gets to let it decide whether a line is dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the paperwork help, and there are enough damaged lines to keep our small crew busy. My mortgage and the children's costs still worry me because we have just over two months of expenses saved, and I'm the junior who has to ask twice on tricky repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking line shifts, check every AI-drafted note against my notebook, and ask for more supervised practice on jointing. In the first year I'd move 35 from each pay into a separate emergency account if our bills allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested in small improvements and fairly comfortable about the job, but the thin household margin catches me. A tool saving ten minutes doesn't pay the mortgage if I miss a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a draft was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a windy call the tool turned 'possible burn at the splice' into 'burn at the splice,' which sounded too certain. I corrected it before my supervisor saw the note, and I marked uncertainty in red in my book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else depends on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner works at a bakery and covers groceries and part of the mortgage, while my wages cover most of the rest. The children are nine and twelve, so even a school activity can upset our neat little budget.

say: I would use **AI drafts** for repeated outage notes while checking safety facts myself.
I would keep human judgment on **live-line status**.
think: I expect **repair demand** to keep the crew working.
Our mortgage and **two-month cushion** make even ordinary absence costly.
do: Keep taking **line shifts** and check drafted notes against the notebook.
Ask for **supervised jointing** practice and transfer 35 per pay if bills allow.
feel: Interested in useful tools, but watchful about the **household margin**.
S0.quote: A tool saving ten minutes doesn't pay the mortgage if I miss a week.
fieldNote: She uses AI **every day**, yet personally corrected an overconfident statement about a damaged splice.
Her comfort with technology sits alongside **junior skill gaps** and a household cushion of just over two months.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and check AI notes against the field notebook
Transfer 35 each pay to an emergency account if bills allow
Ask for supervised jointing practice on line repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot that dispatchers should help test any automated outage map before it sets routes for us. I'd also tell our union rep to push for training places for the office staff whose work gets taken first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The writing and booking jobs could shrink quickly, and that matters to our crews because dispatchers know the back roads and old equipment. Physical line repair moves slower, but I could still lose shifts if the company gives smaller crews more jobs and calls it efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd show the apprentice group how I check AI summaries against the actual pole numbers, and I'd attend the union's dispatch meeting. If the change reaches our depot, I'd trial the approved route tool with my supervisor and ask for a transfer to network inspection if line hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious and a bit protective of the people in the office. I also know curiosity won't help if a roster comes back with two fewer paid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why train others when your own standing is junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the tool's easy part, and I'm honest about the hard electrical part. Last week I found a wrong pole number because I had my muddy notebook beside the screen; that is worth showing the apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a transfer depend on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first ask whether inspection has a paid opening and who supervises new starters. I won't leave a line job for a title with no hours attached.

say: I would involve **dispatchers** in testing automated outage maps.
I would ask the union to defend **office training** as those tasks shrink.
think: I fear lost **local knowledge** if dispatch posts disappear.
I might lose **paid days** if smaller line crews become the norm.
do: Show apprentices how to check **AI summaries** against pole numbers.
Attend the union meeting and trial an **approved route tool**.
Seek a paid **inspection transfer** if line hours fall.
feel: Curious about the tools and **protective** of office colleagues.
S1.quote: I won't leave a line job for a title with no hours attached.
fieldNote: Her curiosity is practical: she compares AI output with **muddy field notes** and teaches that habit.
She links the possible inspection move to **lost line hours** and an actual paid opening.

steps.text: Attend the union meeting about dispatch jobs and training
Trial the approved outage route tool with her supervisor
Request a paid inspection transfer if line hours fall
Show apprentices how to check AI summaries against actual pole numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers that thinking AI by 2028 will reach dispatch and reports before a robot comes near a live line. I'd ask the union for a published crew plan now, because a fast rollout can quietly change paid hours even while we are still climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 45 in 2028 and 48 when capable line robots arrive around 2031, with both children still depending on us. I use AI every day, but that doesn't make me able to outclimb a machine or build another income before the 2028 changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd request the company's equipment trial dates and cancel our second streaming subscription. In 2029 I'd keep taking repairs, volunteer to test approved robotic inspection equipment under a supervisor, and apply to the municipal water team if line shifts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a jolt of fear, then I want to get close enough to the equipment to understand what it actually does. The mortgage means I can't treat a trial as a hobby or work unpaid for an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test on an inspection robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see whether it spots a loose tie on the older crossarms near the canal, because a clean demonstration pole tells me very little. I'd write down every miss before anyone uses its report to send a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my nine-year-old that I still go to work in the bucket for now, and that we're spending less on screens. I'd tell the twelve-year-old honestly that nobody has promised me a job after the robots arrive.

say: I would explain that **2028 office tasks** change before physical repairs.
I would demand a **published crew plan** before paid hours change.
think: I will be **45 then 48** as thinking AI and robots arrive.
My daily AI use cannot guarantee a **line wage** after capable robots.
do: Request **trial dates** and cancel the second streaming subscription.
Keep repairs in **2029** and test approved robotic inspection equipment.
Apply to the **water team** if line shifts are cut.
feel: Frightened by the speed but eager to **inspect the equipment** directly.
S2.quote: I use AI every day, but that doesn't make me able to outclimb a machine or build another income before the 2028 changes.
fieldNote: She separates her **digital confidence** from the threat to physical line work around 2031.
Her test proposal uses an **older crossarm** and recorded misses, while her family budget rules out unpaid work.

steps.text: Cancel the second streaming subscription this month
Volunteer for supervised approved robot trials
Apply to the municipal water team if line shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the utility to train workers and show which jobs remain, not just unveil a machine at the end. I'd push our union to secure paid trial time for the crews and dispatch people together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 when the thinking systems arrive in 2031, and 51 when robots can handle line repairs around 2034. My children will be teenagers or young adults, so school costs will change, but we will still need to cover the mortgage and probably help them start out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office about an electrical testing certificate this winter and put 35 from each pay into savings when possible. If the utility funds a place, I'd enrol; in 2032 I'd still take line shifts and apply for a paid testing role once qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see a route through five years and that makes me more hopeful. I am not sure there will be enough testing posts for everyone, so I wouldn't spend our emergency money on the course myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want supervised time measuring insulation and checking a fault report, because I am still learning the ordinary line work. I'd also ask how many past trainees actually got a paid position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is funded but your schedule is full?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor to swap one overtime shift for class time, if the base pay stays intact. I need a qualification I can use, not a badge that leaves us short on Friday.

say: I would press for **paid trial time** for field and dispatch workers.
I would ask the utility to show **remaining jobs** before robots arrive.
think: I will be **48 in 2031** and 51 when line robots arrive.
Our older children and **mortgage** still leave real costs.
do: Ask about an **electrical testing** certificate this winter.
Save **35 per pay** when possible and enrol if funded.
Keep line shifts in **2032** and apply for a paid testing role if qualified.
feel: More hopeful with time, while wary of **scarce testing posts**.
S3.quote: I need a qualification I can use, not a badge that leaves us short on Friday.
fieldNote: She wants **supervised measurement practice**, reflecting her realistic view of her current skill level.
Her family budget requires **funded class time** and intact base pay before she commits to training.

steps.text: Save 35 per pay when household bills allow
Enrol in electrical testing if the utility funds a place
Apply for a paid testing vacancy after qualifying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us test the machines on real old lines and bargain over what happens to the people they displace. I'd invite the union safety group to keep a public record of failures and fixes, rather than let the vendor grade its own trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, I'll have had time to build skills if the utility lets me, and at 56 in 2039 robots can do the climbing. The children should be grown by then, but I can't count on a pension I haven't checked or on the house being paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue on the line crew, build our savings transfer when bakery hours permit, and take the funded testing certificate if offered. In 2037 I'd apply for a paid network-testing vacancy if I was qualified, while still helping trial approved equipment on the old circuits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years lets me picture doing useful paid work when the bucket belongs to a robot. I still feel wary, because a good trial can become an excuse to end human shifts faster than promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd track missed defects on our oldest circuits alongside the easy new ones and ask crews to sign the results. I'd want the union safety group to see those records before the company changes staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement at 56 solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I haven't looked closely enough at my actual benefits or the remaining mortgage to say that. I'd rather have a paid testing post than make the children our retirement plan.

say: I would seek **worker-checked trials** on old lines throughout the decade.
I would ask the union safety group to see **recorded failures**.
think: I will be **53 then 56** at the two arrival dates.
I cannot assume grown children, a pension or a paid-off **house**.
do: Continue **line shifts** and increase savings when bakery hours permit.
Take a **funded testing** certificate if offered.
Apply for **network-testing work** in 2037 if qualified.
feel: Able to picture useful work, but wary of **premature staffing cuts**.
S4.quote: I'd rather have a paid testing post than make the children our retirement plan.
fieldNote: She wants equipment trials on **old circuits**, with crews recording misses before staffing decisions follow.
Her long plan depends on **paid testing work** and refuses to treat adult children as financial insurance.

steps.text: Keep taking paid line shifts while training
Increase the savings transfer when bakery hours permit
Take the funded electrical testing certificate if offered
Apply for paid network-testing work in 2037 if qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the office changes before our family can build much more savings and robots follow three years later. I'd want a written crew plan, paid trials on real old lines, and funded training that leads to actual jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how we record what a new machine gets wrong. A missing defect can look like a tidy chart until someone has to climb into the dark to fix it.

headlineQuote: A missing defect can look like a tidy chart until someone has to climb into the dark to fix it.
portrait: Lena is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with a mortgage, two school-age children and a working partner.
She uses **AI daily** for notes but checks its wording against her field notebook after finding a dangerous overstatement.
Her savings cover just over **two months**, so she protects wages while seeking supervised practice and funded qualifications.
Across faster scenarios she seeks **worker-led trials** and a route into paid network testing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because office work changes quickly and line robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **written crew plan**, paid trials on old lines and funded training linked to real jobs.
